comparison: Both evaluations support the basic data generation and quality metrics (C1, C2, C38, C39, C40). OpenEval explicitly validates the internal consistency of RNA-seq metrics, while peer reviewers implicitly accepted these by not raising concerns and focusing on analytical approaches instead. Peer review also included C41 (dbSNP validation) in their assessment.

Strong disagreement on eQTL detection claims (C3-C9). OpenEval finds the regulatory variation detection robust with strong statistical support and complementary methods. Peer reviewers express uncertainty, concerned that discoveries might be 'artificially inflated' due to lack of hidden factor correction and potential confounding by population structure.

Both evaluations support the RNA-seq versus array-based genotyping comparison (C10, C11, C67, C68). OpenEval provides detailed validation of the approach, while peer reviewers implicitly accepted these technical comparisons without challenge. OpenEval also included C41 in this grouping.

Disagreement on power decomposition analysis (C12-C16). OpenEval finds the simulation-based approach sound and the multiplicative model well-supported. Peer reviewers express uncertainty, concerned that admixture in the baboon population could explain the observations and potentially inflate discoveries through increased heterozygosity and longer haplotypes.

Both address conservation and eQTL relationships (C17-C19, C43, C44, C56), but with different conclusions. OpenEval finds strong statistical support for conserved patterns of regulatory variation tolerance. Peer reviewers express uncertainty, requesting discussion of whether the negative correlation might be driven by technical issues (only coding SNPs tested, leading to low MAF in conserved genes). Peer review also included C52 in their assessment.

Both address selection versus statistical artifact (C20, C21, C53), but reach different conclusions. OpenEval finds the simulation approach appropriate for distinguishing selection from winner's curse, though notes caution is warranted. Peer reviewers express uncertainty about comparing to Battle et al. 2014, suggesting study differences preclude definitive statements about negative selection in baboons.

Both evaluations support the variance decomposition results (C22-C26, C54). OpenEval validates the permutation-based approach and finds genetic effects well-supported, though notes caution for environmental effects. Peer reviewers did not challenge these findings. Peer review also included C55 in their assessment, while OpenEval addressed C45.

Partial overlap on environmental effects (C26, C55). OpenEval expresses uncertainty about the modest environmental effect and early-life influences due to sample size and multiple testing concerns. Peer reviewers supported the variance partitioning results overall without specific concerns about these claims.

Both address admixture controls (C57-C59), but with different levels of confidence. OpenEval finds the evidence against substantial confounding by population structure adequate. Peer reviewers express uncertainty, noting the existing model 'does not address local patterns of admixture' and requesting additional analyses including tests for excess trans-associations and ASE correlation over longer distances.

Both evaluations support the technical bias assessments (C61-C66). OpenEval systematically validates that reference allele bias and directional effects do not substantially compromise results. Peer reviewers implicitly accepted these controls without challenge.

Both support the novelty claims (C50, C51). OpenEval validates these as appropriate conclusions from the data. Peer reviewers described the study as 'favorably evaluated' and did not challenge the novelty or proof-of-principle demonstration. OpenEval also included C52 in this grouping.

Strong disagreement on hidden factor correction methodology (C42). OpenEval supports the PC-based approach as standard and validated by cited literature. Peer reviewers find this unsupported, explicitly questioning why hidden factor correction was not applied and expressing concern that the PC correction approach was insufficient, potentially leading to artificially inflated discoveries.

OpenEval evaluated claims about human demographic history and its consequences for genetic architecture (C34, C35, C47, C48, C49), finding the literature citations appropriate and connections to study findings logical though somewhat speculative. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.
OpenEval evaluated background and contextual claims from established literature (C27-C33), finding them well-supported and appropriately cited. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.
OpenEval evaluated factual background on the study population (C36, C37), finding them appropriately supported by citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.
OpenEval evaluated the limitation regarding tissue type differences in cross-species comparison (C60), finding the caveat appropriately acknowledged. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.
